question: Under In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2 (Supreme Court of Georgia, 588 S.E.2d 741 (2003)), what did the Court hold regarding who may prepare or facilitate execution of a deed of conveyance and close a Georgia real estate transaction?
choice_a: It is the unauthorized practice of law for anyone other than a duly licensed Georgia attorney to close a real estate transaction or to prepare or facilitate execution of the deed(s), for the benefit of a seller, borrower, or lender
choice_b: Any licensed real estate broker may prepare the deed and close the transaction without attorney involvement
choice_c: A title company employee may prepare and execute the deed as long as the parties consent in writing
choice_d: Only lenders, not sellers or borrowers, require attorney involvement in preparing the deed
explanation: In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2 held that it is the unauthorized practice of law for someone other than a duly licensed Georgia attorney to close a real estate transaction or to prepare or facilitate the execution of the deed(s) for the benefit of a seller, borrower, or lender -- making Georgia an attorney-required closing state.
source_note: In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2, Supreme Court of Georgia, 588 S.E.2d 741 (Ga. 2003)

question: In In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2, why did the Supreme Court of Georgia reject a closing model in which a non-lawyer conducted the closing while an attorney merely 'witnessed' it after the fact?
choice_a: Because the Court found no legal basis to regulate real estate closings at all
choice_b: Because a title company or non-lawyer closing that is only witnessed by an attorney is insufficient -- the attorney must actively conduct or supervise the closing, consistent with the Court's exclusive authority to regulate the practice of law
choice_c: Because witnessed closings were found to be more thorough than attorney-conducted closings
choice_d: Because the Court ruled that only licensed real estate brokers, not attorneys, may supervise closings
explanation: The Court rejected 'lay conveyancing' or witness-only closings, holding that a title company or non-lawyer closing merely witnessed by an attorney does not satisfy the requirement -- the attorney must actively conduct or supervise the closing -- grounding its holding in the Supreme Court of Georgia's exclusive constitutional authority to regulate the practice of law.
source_note: In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2, Supreme Court of Georgia, 588 S.E.2d 741 (Ga. 2003)

question: In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2 rested in part on the Supreme Court of Georgia's prior holdings in two earlier Formal Advisory Opinions. What are they?
choice_a: Formal Advisory Opinion No. 90-1 and Formal Advisory Opinion No. 95-4
choice_b: Formal Advisory Opinion No. 75-2 and Formal Advisory Opinion No. 79-6
choice_c: Formal Advisory Opinion No. 86-5 (86-R9) and Formal Advisory Opinion No. 00-3
choice_d: There were no prior Formal Advisory Opinions cited; the 2003 opinion was a case of first impression
explanation: In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2 cited and relied on the Court's prior holdings in Formal Advisory Opinion No. 86-5 (86-R9), issued May 12, 1989, and Formal Advisory Opinion No. 00-3, issued February 11, 2000, as consistent precedent for requiring attorney involvement in Georgia real estate closings.
source_note: In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2, Supreme Court of Georgia, 588 S.E.2d 741 (Ga. 2003)

question: A Georgia real estate licensee fills in the property description, payment method, special stipulations, and closing date on a standard sales contract form that was originally drafted by legal counsel. Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25.1, does this constitute the unauthorized practice of law?
choice_a: Yes -- only an attorney may ever fill in any blank on a real estate sales contract
choice_b: No, but only if the licensee is also a licensed paralegal
choice_c: Yes -- this carve-out applies only to lease agreements, never to sales contracts
choice_d: No -- licensees are permitted to complete listing/sales contracts or leases on forms prepared by legal counsel, including filling in the property description, payment method, stipulations/addenda, and timing dates, without that constituting UPL
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25.1 expressly permits real estate licensees to complete listing/sales contracts or leases on attorney-prepared forms without that constituting the unauthorized practice of law, including filling in the property description, payment method, special stipulations/addenda, and relevant timing dates.

question: Does the O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25.1 carve-out that lets a Georgia licensee fill in an attorney-prepared sales contract also permit that licensee to prepare the deed of conveyance or conduct the closing itself?
choice_a: No -- the § 43-40-25.1 carve-out is limited to completing listing/sales contracts and leases on attorney-prepared forms; it does not extend to deed preparation or conducting the closing, which under In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2 require a licensed Georgia attorney
choice_b: Yes -- once a licensee may complete a sales contract, the same statute automatically authorizes them to prepare deeds and conduct closings
choice_c: Yes, but only for transactions under a certain sale price
choice_d: No, because O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25.1 does not permit licensees to complete any contract provisions at all
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25.1's carve-out is narrow -- it permits licensees to complete listing/sales contracts and leases on attorney-prepared forms -- but it does not extend to preparing the deed of conveyance or conducting the closing itself, both of which remain governed by In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2's requirement of active attorney conduct or supervision.
source_note: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25.1; In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2, Supreme Court of Georgia, 588 S.E.2d 741 (Ga. 2003)

question: A Georgia buyer's agent, hoping to save the client money, offers to personally draft the warranty deed for an upcoming residential closing and to run the closing meeting herself without any attorney present. Is this permissible under Georgia law?
choice_a: Yes -- any licensed real estate agent may draft deeds and conduct closings in Georgia without restriction
choice_b: No -- under In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2, preparing or facilitating execution of a deed of conveyance and closing a real estate transaction requires the physical involvement of a licensed Georgia attorney; a non-lawyer performing these functions constitutes the unauthorized practice of law
choice_c: Yes, as long as the agent has completed a broker prelicense course
choice_d: Yes, but only if the buyer signs a waiver releasing the agent from liability
explanation: This scenario describes exactly the conduct In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2 prohibits: preparing the deed and conducting the closing without a licensed Georgia attorney's active involvement constitutes the unauthorized practice of law, regardless of the agent's licensure status as a real estate professional.
source_note: In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2, Supreme Court of Georgia, 588 S.E.2d 741 (Ga. 2003)

question: A title company proposes to handle an upcoming Georgia residential closing entirely in-house, with a Georgia-licensed attorney available only to review the file afterward and sign off remotely without attending or actively directing the closing. Does this satisfy In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2?
choice_a: Yes -- as long as an attorney's name appears anywhere on the closing paperwork, the requirement is satisfied
choice_b: Yes -- remote after-the-fact review by any attorney licensed in any state satisfies the requirement
choice_c: No -- the Court rejected closings where a non-lawyer conducts the process and an attorney merely reviews or 'witnesses' after the fact; the attorney must actively conduct or supervise the closing itself
choice_d: No, but only because the attorney must be physically present at the title company's corporate headquarters, regardless of the specific closing location
explanation: In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2 specifically rejected the model of a non-lawyer-conducted closing with only after-the-fact attorney review or 'witnessing' -- the licensed Georgia attorney must actively conduct or supervise the closing, not simply sign off remotely once the process is complete.
source_note: In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2, Supreme Court of Georgia, 588 S.E.2d 741 (Ga. 2003)

question: What is the legal basis the Supreme Court of Georgia relied on in In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2 for its authority to require attorney involvement in real estate closings?
choice_a: A federal statute enacted by Congress specifically governing state real estate closing practices
choice_b: A vote of the Georgia Real Estate Commission adopting the requirement by administrative rule
choice_c: A private industry standard adopted by the State Bar of Georgia's real estate section with no binding legal effect
choice_d: The Supreme Court of Georgia's exclusive constitutional authority to regulate the practice of law
explanation: The Court grounded its holding in the Supreme Court of Georgia's own exclusive authority to regulate the practice of law within the state, rather than in a federal statute, GREC administrative rule, or non-binding industry standard.
source_note: In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2, Supreme Court of Georgia, 588 S.E.2d 741 (Ga. 2003)

question: What is the general purpose of a title search performed before a Georgia closing?
choice_a: To examine the public land records for the property's chain of ownership and identify liens, encumbrances, easements, or other defects that could affect marketable title
choice_b: To determine the buyer's creditworthiness for mortgage approval
choice_c: To calculate the property's ad valorem tax assessment
choice_d: To verify the physical square footage of the structure
explanation: A title search examines recorded land records to trace the chain of title and surface liens, judgments, easements, or other encumbrances that could cloud marketable title, forming the basis for the title commitment and eventual title insurance policy issued at or after closing.

question: What does 'marketable title' generally mean, and why does it matter at a Georgia closing?
choice_a: Title that has been actively advertised for sale by a licensed broker
choice_b: Title reasonably free from defects, liens, and encumbrances such that a reasonably prudent buyer would accept it without fear of litigation, which sellers are typically obligated to deliver at closing
choice_c: Title that has been owned by the same family for at least 20 years
choice_d: Title that has been appraised above the listing price
explanation: Marketable title is title reasonably free of defects and encumbrances that would expose a buyer to litigation risk or an unreasonable challenge to ownership; purchase agreements typically obligate the seller to convey marketable title, which title search and title insurance help verify and protect.

question: What is the key difference between an owner's title insurance policy and a lender's title insurance policy issued in connection with a Georgia closing?
choice_a: An owner's policy and a lender's policy provide identical coverage to the same insured party
choice_b: A lender's policy covers the buyer's personal property inside the home
choice_c: An owner's policy protects the buyer's equity in the property against covered title defects, while a lender's policy protects only the lender's interest up to the loan balance
choice_d: An owner's policy is mandated by Georgia statute on every transaction, while a lender's policy is always optional
explanation: An owner's title insurance policy protects the buyer's ownership interest against covered title defects existing before closing, while a lender's title insurance policy protects only the lender's security interest, generally up to the outstanding loan amount, and does not protect the buyer's equity.

question: Under the TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure rule used nationally for most federally related closed-end mortgage loans, what document must generally be provided to the borrower at least three business days before consummation, itemizing final loan terms and closing costs?
choice_b: The HUD-1 Settlement Statement, unchanged since before the TRID rule took effect
choice_c: The Loan Estimate, provided only at consummation rather than at application
explanation: Under the CFPB's TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure (TRID) rule, the Closing Disclosure itemizes final loan terms and closing costs and generally must be provided to the borrower at least three business days before consummation, having replaced the former HUD-1 settlement statement for most federally related closed-end mortgage loans.
source_note: hedge: standard national closing/settlement content -- federal TRID rule, applies nationwide

question: In a Georgia closing, what are prorations, and why are they used?
choice_a: Adjustments that divide recurring expenses such as property taxes, HOA dues, or prepaid utility costs between buyer and seller based on each party's period of ownership around the closing date
choice_b: A method for splitting the broker's commission between the listing and selling brokerages
choice_c: A calculation used only to determine the buyer's loan-to-value ratio
choice_d: A fee charged exclusively for recording the deed
explanation: Prorations allocate recurring costs such as property taxes, HOA dues, or prepaid utilities between buyer and seller based on how much of the relevant billing period each party will own the property, ensuring neither party bears costs attributable to the other's period of ownership -- a conceptual closing-process mechanic distinct from computing the dollar amounts themselves.

question: Georgia's real estate transfer tax under O.C.G.A. § 48-6-1 is a closing cost typically itemized on the settlement statement. As a matter of market custom rather than statutory mandate, which party customarily pays this tax in Georgia?
choice_a: O.C.G.A. § 48-6-1 expressly requires the buyer, and only the buyer, to pay the transfer tax in every transaction
choice_b: The seller, as a matter of common industry practice and convention, though the statute itself does not dictate which party must pay it
choice_c: The tax is always split 50/50 by statutory formula
choice_d: The buyer's lender is statutorily required to pay the tax on the buyer's behalf
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 48-6-1 sets the transfer tax rate itself but does not dictate which party must pay it; common industry practice in Georgia has the seller pay the transfer tax at closing, though this allocation is a matter of market convention and can be negotiated between the parties, not a fixed statutory requirement.
source_note: O.C.G.A. § 48-6-1 (rate confirmed); customary payer is market convention, not statute

question: At a Georgia closing involving a new security deed, the intangible recording tax under O.C.G.A. § 48-6-61 is charged based on what, and is it typically allocated to the buyer/borrower or the seller as a closing-process matter?
choice_a: It is charged on the sale price of the property and is always paid entirely by the seller
choice_b: It is a flat fee unrelated to the loan amount, paid by the closing attorney out of pocket
choice_c: It is charged on the face amount of the note secured by the security deed, and as the party executing the security deed to obtain financing, the borrower (buyer) is the one who incurs this recording cost at closing
choice_d: It applies only to commercial transactions and never to residential purchase-money security deeds
explanation: The intangible recording tax under O.C.G.A. § 48-6-61 is assessed on the face amount of the note secured by a security deed; because it is the borrower who executes the security deed to secure new financing, this recording cost is conceptually tied to and typically borne in connection with the buyer/borrower's loan closing.

question: Why is prompt recording of the deed with the county after a Georgia closing important to the buyer?
choice_a: Recording is what actually transfers equitable title, before which the buyer has no interest at all
choice_b: Recording is purely a formality with no legal significance once the deed is signed and delivered
choice_c: Recording is required only for commercial property, never for residential property
choice_d: Recording provides constructive public notice of the buyer's ownership interest, helping protect that interest against later claims and generally establishing priority in the public record
explanation: Recording a deed places it in the public record, giving constructive notice of the buyer's ownership and generally establishing priority against later-recorded claims or subsequent purchasers, which is why prompt recording after closing is standard practice.

question: A buyer asks their Georgia agent, 'Do I actually have to involve a lawyer to close on my house?' What is the most accurate response, consistent with In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2?
choice_a: Yes -- Georgia is an attorney-required closing state; a licensed Georgia attorney must actively conduct or supervise the closing and handle the deed of conveyance, unlike states where a title company alone may close the transaction
choice_b: No -- Georgia allows any title company or escrow agent to close a residential transaction without any attorney involvement
choice_c: No -- attorney involvement in Georgia closings is purely optional and a matter of personal preference
choice_d: Yes, but only for commercial transactions; residential closings never require an attorney in Georgia
explanation: Under In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2, Georgia requires the active involvement of a licensed Georgia attorney to prepare/execute the deed and to conduct or supervise the closing, distinguishing Georgia from non-attorney-required states where a title company or escrow agent alone may close the transaction.
source_note: In re UPL Advisory Opinion 2003-2, Supreme Court of Georgia, 588 S.E.2d 741 (Ga. 2003)
